name: Reliability
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Uptime Isn't Optional: Reliability as a Blockchain Design Constraint
lesson.summary: Reliability measures the probability that a system keeps performing its required function correctly over time without failure, and blockchain networks pursue it through replication across many independent operators rather than through one carefully engineered server, which changes both how reliability is achieved and how it can quietly fail.
lesson.body:
Reliability is usually discussed alongside two closely related ideas: availability, whether the system is up and answering requests right now, and correctness, whether the answer it gives is actually right. Conventional software engineering has a long established vocabulary for talking about reliability quantitatively, counting nines of uptime, ninety nine point nine percent, ninety nine point nine nine percent, and so on, each additional nine representing a large drop in the total minutes of downtime tolerated per year. Blockchain systems inherit this same vocabulary as a quality attribute, but they pursue it through a structurally different strategy than a typical web service does.

A conventional application achieves reliability mainly through careful engineering of a small number of servers: redundant hardware, failover systems, a well staffed operations team watching dashboards. A blockchain instead achieves reliability through massive replication across many independently operated nodes scattered around the world, none of which is individually trusted, so that the failure, or even the outright malicious behavior, of any single node does not bring the network down. This is a genuinely different way of buying the same quality attribute, and it is one of the concrete payoffs that decentralization is supposed to provide.

That strategy has a real blind spot, though, and it is worth naming precisely because it is counterintuitive. Replication protects against a node failing independently, from a hard drive dying or an operator losing power, but it does nothing to protect against a bug that exists identically in every node's software, because every node is very often running the same client implementation. A flaw shared by all of them is not diversified away by having thousands of copies. It is a single point of failure that happens to be wearing a decentralized costume. Solana's network experienced several widely reported outages between 2021 and 2022, generally traced to resource exhaustion under heavy transaction load overwhelming validators running the same client software, a documented example of exactly this failure mode: broad replication that did not, on its own, prevent a network wide halt.

This is precisely why maintainability, covered later in this chapter, cares about client diversity, encouraging multiple independent implementations of the same protocol precisely so that a bug in one client's code does not become a bug shared by the entire network. Reliability, in other words, is not purely a function of how many copies of a node exist. It also depends on how independent those copies actually are at the software level, which is a subtler and easier to overlook design decision than simply counting participants.

Reliability also sits in tension with modifiability, the attribute covered just before it. Every upgrade to a blockchain's client software is an opportunity to introduce a new bug, so a network that changes frequently to stay modifiable is, all else equal, exposed to more reliability risk than one that changes rarely. Neither extreme, freezing the software forever or upgrading constantly, is obviously correct, and resolving that tension deliberately, rather than by default, is exactly the kind of decision a utility tree exercise is meant to force into the open.
